summary: A 1979 request for comments on ideas for naming, addressing and delivery in ARPANET message systems. It is not a specification of a protocol about to be implemented but a set of concepts for the next generation of mail systems.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 757 proposes separating who a mail recipient is from where their mailbox is located. It sketches persistent IDs, a distributed directory, and delivery steps but asks for comments rather than specifying an implementation.

questions: how does rfc 757 separate names from addresses
subtitle: A request for comments on separating a mail recipient's identity from delivery addresses.

tldr.problem: The ARPANET mail address combined a user's name and location, so changing a mailbox location could change the user's address and make old mail undeliverable.
tldr.mechanism: The paper proposes persistent recipient IDs, a network database mapping IDs to delivery addresses, and local databases that cache useful information.
tldr.outcome: The author explicitly presents this as a request for comments on concepts for a future message system, not as a protocol specification.

today: RFC 757 is a request for comments on concepts for a next generation of message systems. Its preface explicitly says it is not a specification of a protocol about to be implemented.

sections.title: The Naming and Addressing Problem
sections.content:
The memo says the current USERNAME@HOST form does not clearly distinguish a recipient's identity from the delivery point. If users change hosts, their names and addresses may change, and messages sent to old addresses can become undeliverable.

The existing delivery system is described as a simple extension of FTP, handling a single message to a single user. The author says bundling messages and delivering them to multiple recipients could improve it.
sections.plainLanguage: The address says both who should receive mail and where to deliver it. If the mailbox moves, the address can stop working.

sections.title: Persistent IDs and a Distributed Directory
sections.content:
The proposal assigns each authorized recipient a unique ID that remains with the user as their address or affiliation changes. A network database maps each ID to one or more delivery addresses and may include information such as the owner's name and affiliation.

Rather than require every host to keep a complete database, local systems can keep mini-databases and consult the network database when a local entry is missing. They can store returned information locally for later use.
sections.plainLanguage: A recipient's ID stays the same even if the delivery address changes. A local mail system can look up the address and keep a local copy of the information.

sections.title: Delivery and Mail Processing
sections.content:
Delivery has three parts: find an address for the recipient ID, send the message, and let the receiving host process it. The proposal allows bulk mail to several recipients, bundled messages for one recipient, or combinations of those options.

The receiving host may sort messages, distribute copies to multiple destinations, or perform other local functions. The memo leaves the design of those mail-room functions to each host.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender looks up a delivery address, sends the message, and the receiving host handles it. The receiving host can sort or copy messages according to its own services.

sections.title: Scope and Relationship to Other Proposals
sections.content:
The preface states that RFC 757 is not a specification for a protocol about to be implemented. It asks for comments on concepts that might help design the next generation of message creation and delivery systems.

The memo discusses a relationship to RFC 753's internetwork message delivery system and says the proposals are not incompatible: one concentrates on communication across different host protocols, while this paper focuses on delivery within a common protocol environment.
sections.plainLanguage: This paper is a design discussion, not an implementation specification. It describes how its database-based addressing idea could complement an internetwork message system.
